title: Verbal daggers
hookLine: the monks at Kosambi quarrel, stabbing each other with words; six things that make for harmony
tomorrow: The god who thought he was permanent

cards: A group chat goes sideways. Someone says something sharp, someone screenshots it, and by evening nobody remembers what started it, only who said what. It's an old story.
In the city of Kosambi, the Buddha's own monks split into two camps. The monastic rule books say it began over something small.
By the time the Buddha heard about it, the discourse says, they were stabbing each other with verbal daggers.

teach.b: This is the forty-eighth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the discourse at Kosambi. The Buddha calls the monks in and asks a quiet question.

teach.h: KINDNESS IN DEED, WORD AND THOUGHT
teach.b: When you quarrel like this, are you acting toward each other with kindness, in deed, word and thought, openly and in private? No, they say. Then what do you know, what do you see, that you quarrel like this?
It will lead to your harm for a long time. Then he gives six qualities that create love and respect and lead to harmony and unity. Kindness in deed toward your companions, openly and in private.
Kindness in word. Kindness in thought.

teach.h: SHARE EVEN WHAT'S IN YOUR BOWL
teach.b: Sharing what you receive, even what's in your bowl, with those who keep the precepts. Keeping the same virtue as your companions, whole and unbroken. And sharing a view that leads out of suffering.
Look at the first three. They come before anything about who's right. You don't have to settle the argument to stop stabbing.
You put the dagger down first, and then talk. The fourth is so practical: share your food. It's hard to stay at war with someone whose bowl you've just filled.

teach.h: THE SHARED VIEW IS THE ROOF PEAK
teach.b: The last, the shared view, the Buddha says, is like the roof peak of a house, the part that holds the rest together.
But he starts at the door, with kindness of hand and mouth and heart. The six are often called the qualities of warm remembrance: a recipe for living with people you disagree with.

how: Buddhist monasteries and lay communities study the six qualities of warm remembrance (saraniya dhamma) from MN 48 as guidance for living in harmony, especially when disagreements arise.

o: a sharp debate that finds the truth
words used to wound, as in a quarrel
a monk's vow of total silence

games.q: the six for harmony — tap the pairs.
p: kindness in deed, word and thought
share even what's in your bowl
a shared view: the roof peak

s: the Buddha first decided which camp was right
he asked whether they were acting with kindness, and gave six qualities for harmony.
sharing food is one of the six qualities
sharing what you receive, even what's in your bowl, with companions who keep the precepts.
the six qualities are about private feelings only
the first three are kindness in deed, word and thought, both openly and in private.

games.q: two camps of monks are stabbing each other with words. you're the Buddha. what do you ask them first?
o: are you acting toward each other with kindness?
games.why: he asks about kindness in deed, word and thought. they say no. then he teaches six things that make for harmony.

practice: Think of a little friction still in the air, a sharp text, a cold silence, a disagreement at work, and picture the other person without deciding who was right.
Picture setting the dagger down, your words, your tone, and find one kind sentence you could offer first. Hold that for a few breaths, and rest.

wordCard.voice: Verbal daggers. Words used to stab, as the monks of Kosambi did, and six qualities that put them down.

orig.note: Pali saraniya: to be remembered, warmly recalled. the six saraniya dhamma are qualities for harmony.

carryVoice: Your line: verbal daggers down. Kindness first, and then the talking can begin. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 48, Kosambiya Sutta (the discourse at Kosambi)
